terms.grammar: quā, by which way; ītur, impersonal passive of eō
terms.comment: Our sentence, made of two classical uses: quā “by which way” (Lewis & Short), and the impersonal ītur ad, “one goes to”, as in Vergil’s sīc ītur ad astra (A. 9.641). We have found no set question for this in the authors we searched or in Traupman, Morgan–Owens, or Levi–Bini; Traupman’s nearest is quā viā (p. 201). Where the choice is between two roads, Plautus’s people ask hāc an illāc?.

evidence: Plaut. Rud. 213: ita nunc hāc an illāc eam, incerta sum cōnsilī
Plaut. Cist. 679: utrum hāc an illāc iter īnstiterit

phrases.latin: saltem aliquem velim quī mihi ex hīs locīs aut viam aut sēmitam mōnstret, ita nunc hāc an illāc eam, incerta sum cōnsilī
phrases.english: I wish at least there were someone to show me a road or a path out of this place: as it is, I can’t make up my mind whether to go this way or that

phrases.latin: dextera quae Dītis magnī sub moenia tendit, hāc iter Ēlysium nōbīs
phrases.english: the right-hand road, which runs under the walls of great Dis: this way lies our road to Elysium

phrases.latin: Magister, quā viā Rōmānī antīquitus in Graeciam iter faciēbant?
phrases.english: Teacher, by what way did the Romans travel to Greece in ancient times?
Which way is it to the harbour, please?
How do I get from here to the harbour?

sources: Lewis & Short: qua · Lewis & Short: eo · Lewis & Short: illac
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 201.
